data.title: Engineering Ethics
data.subtitle: Week 1: Fundamental Principles and Decision Frameworks

narr: Welcome to our exploration of engineering ethics. In this section, we'll cover the fundamental principles that guide ethical behavior in engineering, from the NSPE canons to personal ethical frameworks.
We'll also examine practical decision-making tools to help navigate complex ethical situations you might encounter in your engineering career.

data.heading: The Ten Canons of Engineering Ethics
bullets: Safety first — the safety, health and welfare of the public comes before everything
Stay in your lane — work only within your area of competence
Speak truthfully — public statements only objective and truthful
No conflicts of interest — be a faithful agent, do not allow personal interest to conflict with duty
No deception — avoid all deceptive acts

narr: The first canon emphasizes that safety must always come first. This is paramount in all engineering decisions.
Second, engineers should only work within their area of competence, ensuring they have the necessary knowledge and skills.
Truthfulness in all public statements is essential for maintaining trust in the profession.
Avoiding conflicts of interest helps maintain objectivity and professional integrity.
Deceptive acts of any kind are prohibited, as they undermine the foundation of engineering practice.
Let's start with the ten canons of engineering ethics, adapted from the NSPE code. These provide a comprehensive framework for ethical behavior in engineering practice.

data.heading: The Ten Canons of Engineering Ethics (cont.)
bullets: Act honorably — behave responsibly, protecting the reputation of the profession
No hidden payments — do not take payment from more than one interested party without full consent
Don't misrepresent yourself — never falsify your qualifications, experience or results
Give proper credit — acknowledge the real contribution of others
Don't stay silent — report, or refuse to approve, violations of the norms, even under pressure

narr: Honorably behavior includes protecting the reputation of the engineering profession as a whole.
Financial transparency is maintained by avoiding hidden payments that could compromise professional judgment.
Engineers must accurately represent their qualifications and experience without exaggeration.
Proper credit must be given to others' contributions, respecting intellectual property.
Finally, engineers have a responsibility to report violations, even when facing pressure to remain silent.

data.heading: Five Cornerstones of Personal Ethical Behavior
bullets: Do what you say you will do
Never disclose information given to you in confidence
Take responsibility for your actions (and mistakes)
Never participate in a lie
Never accept gifts that would compromise your ability to act in the best interests of your organization

narr: Beyond the formal canons, personal ethical behavior rests on five cornerstones.
First, reliability through keeping commitments builds trust in professional relationships.
Confidentiality is essential for maintaining trust in professional interactions.
Taking responsibility, including acknowledging mistakes, demonstrates professional maturity.
Honesty requires never participating in lies, even when convenient.
Finally, avoiding compromising gifts maintains objectivity in decision-making.
It's worth noting that these cornerstones don't explicitly include the 'golden rule' found in many ethical traditions: 'Do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself'.

data.heading: Top 10 Questions for Ethical Decision Making
bullets: Would I do this in front of my mother?
Does this choice lead to the greatest good for the greatest number of people?
How will it make me feel about myself?
Is it fair, balanced and honest?
If something terrible happens, will I be able to defend my actions?

narr: The first question is perhaps the most straightforward: would you do this in front of your mother?
Consider whether your choice leads to the greatest good for the greatest number of people.
Reflect on how this decision will affect your self-perception and integrity.
Evaluate whether the decision is fair, balanced, and honest in all respects.
Consider whether you could defend your actions if something terrible were to happen.
When facing ethical dilemmas, consider these ten questions in order, starting with the most important.

data.heading: Top 10 Questions for Ethical Decision Making (cont.)
bullets: Would it withstand public scrutiny?
Is it right?
Is it safe?
Is it legal?
Could the decision become a habit?

narr: Public scrutiny is another important factor - would your decision withstand public examination?
The fundamental question of whether something is right should guide your decision.
Safety considerations must always be paramount in engineering decisions.
Legality provides a baseline requirement for any professional decision.
Finally, consider whether this decision could become a habit - if yes, don't do it.

data.heading: The Engineering Ethics Decision Matrix
bullets: Rows represent the NSPE canons
Columns represent possible courses of action
Cells indicate whether an action satisfies each canon (yes/no/maybe)
Sum 'yes' and 'no' answers across each column
The action with the most 'yes' answers is recommended
Exception: if one criterion overrides all others, follow it

narr: The Engineering Ethics Decision Matrix is a practical tool for analyzing ethical dilemmas.
The rows of the matrix represent the NSPE canons we discussed earlier.
The columns represent different possible courses of action you might take.
Each cell indicates whether a particular action satisfies a specific canon, with answers of yes, no, or maybe.
After filling the matrix, sum the 'yes' and 'no' answers across each column, ignoring the 'maybes'.
The action with the most 'yes' answers is generally recommended by this approach.
However, there's an important exception: if one criterion overrides all others, you should follow that criterion regardless of the matrix results.

data.text: To give the utmost of performance; to participate in none but honest enterprise; to live and work according to the laws of man and the highest standards of professional conduct; to place service before profit, the honor and standing of the profession before personal advantage, and the public welfare above all other considerations

narr: The Engineer's Creed, established by the NSPE in 1954, encapsulates the professional commitment of engineers.
It emphasizes giving maximum performance, participating only in honest enterprises, and adhering to both legal and professional standards.
The creed prioritizes service over profit, professional honor over personal advantage, and public welfare above all considerations.

data.heading: Key Engineering Ethics Terms
bullets: Academic dishonesty: cheating, plagiarism, marking attendance for another person
Plagiarism: presenting someone else's work as your own without citation
Conflict of interest: a clash between personal interests and the duties of a position
Contract: a voluntary agreement of two or more parties; legally binding
Professional responsibility: the responsibility connected with possessing specialized knowledge and using it for the benefit of society

narr: Let's clarify some key terms in engineering ethics.
Academic dishonesty includes various forms of cheating, plagiarism, and dishonest practices like marking attendance for others.
Plagiarism specifically involves presenting someone else's work as your own without proper attribution.
A conflict of interest occurs when personal interests clash with professional duties, potentially compromising objectivity.
A contract is a legally binding voluntary agreement between two or more parties.
Professional responsibility acknowledges that specialized knowledge comes with the duty to use it for society's benefit.

data.heading: Week 1 Question 1
data.problem: Why do you want to become an engineer?
data.result: Strong answers connect personal motives to the definition of engineering: "I want to be one of the people who turn scientific knowledge into working solutions"

narr: Let's look at some questions from week 1 that explore your motivations for engineering.
First question: why do you want to become an engineer?
The model answer suggests reflecting on three typical motives: an inspiring person, a specific problem you wanted to solve, or a favorite school subject.
A strong answer connects your personal motive to the definition of engineering.
For example: "I want to be one of the people who turn scientific knowledge into working solutions".

data.heading: Week 1 Question 2
data.problem: Which field of engineering interests you the most? Why did you choose exactly this one?

steps.text: Name your chosen field of engineering
Connect it to specific products from lecture
Relate to a NAE Grand Challenge

data.result: Model justification: name the field (e.g., energy/electrical), connect to specific products (power, circuits, control systems), relate to NAE Grand Challenge (e.g., "make solar energy economical"), and mention professional society (e.g., IEEE)

narr: Second question: which field of engineering interests you most and why?
Any answer is acceptable as this is an introduction to your interests.
A model justification includes naming your chosen field.
Then connect it to specific products mentioned in the lecture.
Relate your choice to a National Academy of Engineering Grand Challenge.
Finally, mention the relevant professional society for that field.
